title: Sandbox persistence is now GA
description:
Vercel Sandboxes now automatically save and restore filesystem state between sessions. Persistence is on by default, meaning no snapshots to manage or state to track manually.

Each sandbox has a durable, customizable name that acts as a unique reference in your project. You can create, retrieve, or resume a sandbox by name. Vercel spins sessions up and down automatically, without interrupting your workflow.

Create a persistent sandbox

When you call Sandbox.create(), persistence is enabled by default:

Each automatic snapshot consumes snapshot storage, which is billed separately from compute. For ephemeral workloads, opt out of persistence to minimize storage costs:

To opt out of persistence with the CLI, pass --non-persistent to sandbox create. Non-persistent sandboxes discard their filesystem when the session ends.

Resume a persistent sandbox

Resuming is automatic. Any call on a stopped sandbox, like runCommand() or writeFiles(), starts a new session from the most recent snapshot.

Other improvements

  • Sandbox.fork(): Create a new sandbox from an existing one

  • Sandbox.getOrCreate(): Idempotent retrieve-or-create for long-lived sandboxes

  • Sandbox.delete(): Permanently delete a sandbox

  • Richer sandbox.stop(): Returns snapshot metadata plus active-CPU and network-transfer totals

  • Lifecycle hooks: onCreate and onResume hooks for create, get, and getOrCreate

  • Tags: Assign custom properties to sandboxes for multi-tenant tracking

Get started

Upgrade to the latest version to create persistent sandboxes by default:

  • pnpm install @vercel/sandbox@latest # SDK

  • pnpm install -g sandbox@latest # CLI

Learn more about persistent sandboxes in the documentation.

title: How Conductor moved parallel coding agents from the laptop to the cloud with Vercel Sandbox
description:
Conductor on Vercel

  • Multiple parallel coding agents running at scale in the cloud

  • Model-agnostic, works with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents

  • Used by engineering teams at Notion, Linear, Ramp, and Life360

Interacting with a single coding agent feels natural, and Conductor makes directing a fleet of agents just as intuitive.

It's a GUI for spinning up multiple coding agents in parallel, each working on an isolated branch of your codebase at once. You review their work, merge what works, and redirect the agents that need to keep iterating.

Engineering teams loved it, but hardware was a real limitiation. Every agent ran on your machine, so the fan climbed, the CPU ran hot, and if you closed your laptop, the agents stopped.

Charlie Holtz, co-founder and CEO of Conductor, spent time at Vercel before starting the company. He understands what developers lose when their environment imposes rules on how they can work. Cloud Workspaces, Conductor's remote execution layer built on Vercel Sandboxes, removes the local hardware constraint. Developers can now spawn multiple agents and close the lid without interrupting work.

The journey from local to cloud

Developers who adopted Conductor early felt the power. Notion's engineering team said, "It makes you feel like an octopus, where each one of your arms is working on something separately."

The demand for remote execution came quickly. Developers wanted more agents running longer, and local hardware was the ceiling. For a six-person startup, going from local to cloud is a huge technical leap, and when the developers using Conductor work at companies like Linear and Ramp, provider choice is a matter of building trust with engineers choosing to run their code on infrastructure they don't own.

The team evaluated several sandbox providers, weighing fast spin-up and snapshot support alongside longevity and the depth of the support relationship.

Running parallel agents in the cloud

Conductor built Cloud Workspaces on Vercel Sandboxes. When a developer opens a new workspace, agents spin up on a remote server instead of their local machine. The interface doesn't change.

Holtz describes the result: "To our users it feels just like the local version of Conductor. They don't know the difference, which is amazing, and that's because Vercel Sandboxes are super fast."

Conductor already supports Claude Code, Codex and other coding agents, but they are model agnostic. That means that no matter how often labs release updates, or what the next popular harness is, they can keep the same cloud layer underneath. As Holtz puts it: "The vibes shift every 3 months. Right now GPT-5.5 has the vibes on its side, but that's going change in another few months. Being agnostic to the providers is the key, and we get that with Vercel."

One interface, whatever the frontier looks like next

Conductor's bet is on the interface: the one place to direct your agents, review their work, and decide what to merge. With Vercel Sandbox, that interface goes wherever developers go.

About Conductor: Conductor is a multi-agent IDE for running coding agents in parallel, each on isolated branches of your codebase. Model-agnostic by design, it works with Claude Code, Codex, and other coding agents.

title: Team-wide provider allowlist on AI Gateway
description:
AI Gateway now supports a team-wide provider allowlist. Teams can restrict which providers can serve requests, so traffic only routes to approved providers. The allowlist applies to every request through AI Gateway, including Bring Your Own Key (BYOK) traffic.

Regulated teams typically vet AI providers across multiple dimensions with security and legal sign-off, ending up with a vendor set that reflects the specific requirements of their org. The allowlist turns that approved-vendor list into a routing guarantee:

  • Enforcement happens at the gateway level, not at the request level. A developer on the team cannot route traffic to a provider the org hasn't approved.

  • This restriction also applies to coding agents. Even if an agent omits or modifies request-level provider filters, AI Gateway still blocks unapproved providers.

  • Only team owners can modify the provider allowlist, keeping control centralized and auditable.

  • New providers are disabled by default once the allowlist is on, so the approved set doesn't silently expand when AI Gateway integrates a new vendor.

How to configure

Toggle on Provider Allowlist in the AI Gateway Settings tab. All current providers are allowed by default, so existing traffic is unaffected. Disable any providers your team shouldn't use.

The allowlist filters by provider, not by model. AI Gateway falls back to other allowed providers for the same model if the initial provider fails. The allowlist also functions as an and with other restrictions applied to the team, like Zero Data Retention (ZDR) or request-level filtering.

For example, if a team has disabled DeepSeek in their allowlist and a request pins routing to only the DeepSeek provider:

Since DeepSeek is not in the allowlist, AI Gateway rejects the request.

Provider Allowlist works across every API format supported by AI Gateway, including AI SDK, OpenAI Chat Completions API, and Anthropic Messages API.

Read the provider allowlist documentation for more information. For other account-level security and compliance functionality, check the Zero Data Retention and Disallow Prompt Training documentation.

title: Protecting against token theft
description:
HTTP requests are inexpensive. Vercel charges ~$2/million, a fraction of a cent per call. But a single prompt to an agent on a frontier model can cost $2, making AI a million times more expensive, and inference theft one of the highest-margin businesses an attacker can run. We have seen this type of attack on our own APIs.

If you have AI endpoints exposed to the internet, the risk of abuse is high and can easily run up bills in the tens of thousands of dollars or more.

Protecting those endpoints requires verification to run on every AI request, not on the session or signup. Rate limits and auth walls aren't sufficient on their own because checks that run once per session get amortized away across thousands of stolen calls.

At Vercel, we gate every AI request through BotID deep analysis, and you can do the same on your own endpoints with a few lines of code.

What inference theft is

Inference theft is the unauthorized use of someone else's paid AI inference, either for free consumption or downstream resale. The operator pays per AI call; the attacker pays nothing for inference and then resells the tokens at a discount. This goes beyond rate-limit abuse to actual resale of a stolen resource in a market.

Which AI endpoints are at risk?

Any internet-facing endpoint that gives a caller meaningful control over an LLM prompt is a target. The more general the endpoint, the higher the payout per stolen call.

AI playgrounds, like the AI SDK Playground, are the most dangerous shape because the caller has maximum control over the prompt, the model, and often the parameters. Stolen calls land cleanly into any standard client.

Support bots and documentation assistants are less exposed when system prompts are fixed server-side, but attackers have learned how to talk the models around system prompts cheaply enough to make resale viable.

Resale value tracks how easily the stolen calls can be dropped into a provider-compatible client.

Why web defenses don't mitigate inference theft

IP rate limits and auth walls were built to defend against attacks with dramatically lower per-call economics, where gaming IPs and accounts weren't worth the cost.

The payoff from stolen inference is high enough that attackers will procure residential proxy IPs by the thousands and register throwaway accounts at whatever scale it takes to defeat your gate. Rate limits get diluted across the fleet of IP addresses, and real accounts pass authentication.

The architecture of abuse

Sophisticated attackers wrap your custom AI endpoint in an OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible adapter and fan calls out through residential proxies.

The adapter is the key component. It is a one-time engineering cost that presents the victim's idiosyncratic API as OpenAI- or Anthropic-compatible, so stolen inference can drop into any standard coding agent or SDK. Reselling at even five to ten percent of the list price, with zero marginal inference cost, can make for a generous-margin business.

A recent example is Chipotlai Max, a forked coding agent that ships with a proxy turning Chipotle's customer-support chatbot into an OpenAI-compatible endpoint. The project openly solicits help in porting the same inference-theft approach to Home Depot, Lowe's, Target, and Starbucks.

The adapter also serves as the session boundary for the attacker's downstream users. They authenticate to the adapter, not to your endpoint. By the time a call hits your API, it has already crossed the boundary you were planning to defend. The check has to run on the call the adapter proxies, not on the session it sits behind.

The shape of a real attack on our own endpoint

On April 12, 2026, traffic to the Vercel docs AI chat endpoint spiked to roughly ten times normal volume on Anthropic's Claude Haiku 4.5 model. Traffic rose to 1,300 requests per minute at peak, which would have translated to an inference cost run rate of over ten thousand dollars per day.

The attack came in through residential proxies that obscured the real client IPs. Across hundreds of thousands of bot requests over two days, standard per-IP rate limits had nothing useful to act on.

How to defend against inference theft

Protecting AI endpoints against inference theft requires verification of every request. We use Vercel's BotID with deep analysis, called inside the route handler before the AI request lands.

Verification has to run on every AI request

If our gate had run at session start instead of per request, the attacker would have paid the bypass cost once and walked away with hundreds of thousands of stolen calls. Any check that runs per session amortizes the attacker's bypass cost across every subsequent inference call. Per-request gates force that ratio down to one, and even at high inference prices, defeating a check on every call isn't worth the cost.

This is where the cost asymmetry works in the defender's favor. Inference is the most expensive resource per call that the attacker steals, but verification is one of the cheapest protection costs per call.

Implementing request verification with BotID deep analysis

Traditional image CAPTCHAs no longer hold up against modern attackers because the same AI models that make inference worth stealing can easily bypass them.

We deploy Vercel BotID on our AI endpoints, gating every request. BotID is an invisible CAPTCHA with deep analysis powered by Kasada that uses client-side machine learning to distinguish humans from bots without a visible challenge, so it can run on every request rather than only at session start.

BotID deep analysis detected and blocked more than ten thousand bot requests in the first minutes of the spike. Within twenty-four hours, request volume on the endpoint was flat at normal levels.

Server-side, checkBotId() runs inside the route handler and returns a classification for the request currently being served.

The route also has to be declared on the client. Without this, checkBotId() fails because BotID doesn't attach the challenge headers to the request:

See the BotID docs for the next.config.ts wrapper and the full setup.

Protect inference, not just access

Inference will remain orders of magnitude more expensive than the requests it carries, so resale will remain profitable, and attackers will keep iterating.

To protect your AI endpoints:

  • Audit which of your AI endpoints are exposed

  • Prioritize by attack likelihood: more caller prompt control means an easier target

  • Gate every endpoint on every request

title: Signed URLs are now available for Vercel Blob
description:
You can now generate time-bound signed URLs for Vercel Blob. A signed URL is a scoped URL with an expiry that allows you to upload, download, inspect, or delete a specific object without giving access to your entire Blob store.

Each URL is scoped to a single operation (put, get, head, or delete), a single pathname, and an expiry you choose, up to 7 days. The signature covers the operation and constraints, so a URL signed for a GET can't be reused as a PUT.

Direct uploads from the browser

Upload URLs (put) support multipart, so the browser can stream large files straight to Blob storage without round-tripping through your server.

Conditional deletes

Delete URLs accept an ifMatch option so the delete only applies if the object hasn't been overwritten since you signed the URL:

Signed URLs work alongside OIDC. Your server authenticates to Blob via OIDC, generates a signed token, and produces narrowly scoped, time-bound URLs for the browser, so your long-lived BLOB_READ_WRITE_TOKEN never leaves the server.

Update @vercel/blob to 2.4.0 and read the documentation to get started.

title: Updates to Legal Terms
description:
The proliferation of agentic workflows means developers now regularly grant AI tools direct access to their infrastructure, use services that act autonomously, and build on platforms that themselves use AI to operate. We’ve updated our Terms of Service and Marketplace terms to clarify shared responsibility when actions on your account may be taken by AI, whether Vercel's own or a third-party tool you've connected, as well as other important updates detailed below.

What is changing?

AI Functionality and Third-Party Tools

Vercel's platform increasingly includes AI-powered services, including v0, Vercel Agent, WAF natural language rules, and AI Gateway. These services may take actions on your behalf. We've introduced two new concepts to make the responsibilities around this explicit:

AI Functionality refers to Vercel services that are AI-powered, that help you build AI products (like AI SDK), or that connect to AI providers (like AI Gateway).

Third-Party Tools refers to any non-Vercel tool, script, service, or automation (AI-powered or not) that you grant access to your Vercel account. This includes CI/CD pipelines, third-party agents, and integration scripts.

The key responsibilities:

  • You control how AI Functionality behaves through your settings. Those settings define the scope of what AI Functionality can do on your behalf.

  • You are responsible for reviewing and authorizing the actions AI Functionality takes, and for evaluating its outputs against your own requirements.

  • If you grant a Third-Party Tool access to your Vercel account (e.g., giving it your API key), you are responsible for what it does, including any costs it incurs.

  • You are responsible for actions taken by AI Functionality or Third-Party Tools on your behalf.

Billing flexibility

We are updating our billing terms to reflect the expansion of our product surface area beyond subscription plans.

  • Fees are no longer exclusively tied to a subscription plan. Services like AI Gateway credits can be purchased and charged independently.

  • For non-subscription services, charges may occur at the time of purchase or top-up.

  • If your account shows unusually high or suspicious usage, Vercel may charge accrued fees ahead of your regular billing cycle. Learn more about Partial Invoices.

We have also added a direct link to vercel.com/pricing in the terms.

Enterprise Managed Accounts

Enterprise customers who have verified ownership of an email domain can now claim email addresses on that domain that are associated with existing Vercel accounts. If your account email falls within a claimed domain, Vercel will notify you and you'll have the option to update your email address. If the account was used for work with that organization, it may instead be added to their Team. In either case, the Enterprise customer does not gain access to your account or your content without your consent.

Representations

Two new customer representations have been added:

  • You confirm you have the rights to provide any third-party credentials or API keys to Vercel (for example, through Vercel Connect or other integrations).

  • You confirm you are not subject to applicable OFAC sanctions.

Marketplace

The Marketplace terms now introduce the concept of Authorized Users, which includes Third-Party Tools. Actions taken by Authorized Users are bound to you as the customer, and you are responsible for reporting any unauthorized Authorized User activity.

Privacy Policy

We have updated the Data Privacy Framework section. Previously, unresolved EU/UK/Swiss privacy complaints were directed to data protection authorities. We've now designated VeraSafe as our private complaint handler. Complaints can be submitted directly to VeraSafe before escalation to a regulator.

Frequently asked questions

The full updated Terms of Service are at vercel.com/legal/terms. The Marketplace terms and Privacy Policy are linked from the same page.

title: DeepSeek enters the fight for token volume, Anthropic continues to dominate spend
description:
AI Gateway Production Index — June 2026

Every month, AI Gateway routes tens of trillions of tokens between production applications and AI labs, giving us visibility into what AI usage actually looks like, separate from leaderboards and benchmarks. We publish the data monthly in the AI Gateway production index.

June 2026 summary

The July index reports on AI Gateway data collected in May 2026.

  • Total AI Gateway tokens grew +20% MoM; total spend grew +43% MoM. Customers paid almost 20% more per token on average than in April.

  • DeepSeek’s share of tokens jumped from under 1% to 17% in a single month, while its share of spend stayed near 1%.

  • Anthropic’s share of spend grew from 61% to 65% in May, holding 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case (AI app generation, back office agents, and coding agents).

  • Cost-consciousness meant smarter routing between low-cost and frontier models. Customers got more deliberate about which model did which work, while overall usage kept climbing.

Last month, headlines about blown token budgets dominated tech news: Uber burned through its annual Claude Code budget shortly after Q1 and Amazon shut down KiroRank to curb unproductive tokenmaxxing. While runaway cost is a real problem, this month’s report shows that spend on production use cases still increased.

Two insights emerged from AI Gateway data in May:

  • Low-cost models entered production: New models shipped at price points that made the established labs look even more expensive, and they are capable enough to enter the mix in production.

  • Spend is increasing, but with smarter model mixes: Teams are still increasing token budgets, but they are implementing smarter routing strategies to get more value out of every dollar.

Low-cost models saw significant production volume for the first time

From February to April, volume distribution across labs on AI Gateway changed slowly, but in May, DeepSeek V4's launch completely shifted token share. The low-cost end of the market that barely existed in April became AI Gateway’s third-largest provider by volume in May, without a significant impact on overall spend.

In April, DeepSeek accounted for less than 1% of AI Gateway tokens and less than 0.2% of spend. In May, its volume share jumped to 17% of tokens, putting it in third place, ahead of OpenAI. Almost all of the volume comes from two models: deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash and deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro, both released in May.

The spend picture tells the other half of the story. Even though DeepSeek’s token share grew to 17% in a single month, its cost share stayed near 1%.

DeepSeek V4 Flash launched at $0.14 input / $0.28 output per million tokens, roughly 20–50× lower than comparable Anthropic models and 8–12× lower than other value-tier flagships like Qwen 3.6 Plus and Kimi K2.6. With a savings gap that big, teams adopted V4 Flash quickly.

Price alone wouldn’t have shifted DeepSeek’s volume that much in a month, meaning teams testing DeepSeek V4 against their existing evals found the output good enough to ship, not just low-cost enough to try.

Value-tier models have always been available on AI Gateway, but have never captured token share at this scale, meaning DeepSeek V4 was the first model at its price point to clear the quality bar for production work.

Frontier labs continued to capture a majority of new spend

Even as the low-cost end of the market grew fastest in volume, the expensive end grew faster in dollars.

Anthropic’s token share grew from 26% to 32%, and its spend share from 61% to 65%. OpenAI’s token share held near 13%, but its spend share ticked up from 12% to 13% on a much larger total, so customers were paying more per OpenAI token in May.

The average token got more expensive in May, even with DeepSeek pulling the average down. That increase happened because the work that demands frontier models grew faster than the work that doesn’t. The AI coding agent use case shows the low-cost/frontier split most clearly:

  • DeepSeek drove 49% of the segment’s token volume, but only 4% of the cost.

  • Anthropic drove 28% of tokens and 70% of the cost.

Lower-cost models are now a meaningful part of production workflows, but frontier model use is still growing, driving the increase in overall spend.

The frontier is getting more expensive per token, and customers are still paying. Anthropic continues to lead on spend, taking 65% of all gateway spend in May, and 70–80% of spend across every high-stakes use case.

Cost discipline became a routing strategy

Increased overall spend showed that demand for AI continued to grow in May, but teams applied more precision to their budgets through routing. They sent the cheap, high-volume work to lower-priced models and used frontier models where quality mattered most. Slow adoption of Google's latest Flash model is a clear example.

Gemini 3.5 Flash launched in May at a higher price point than Gemini 3.0 Flash, but migration didn’t happen at scale. By month-end, 3.5 held only 7% of the Flash family’s tokens while 3.0 held 90%.

Compared to the rapid adoption of Gemini 3.1 Pro across February and March, slower migration to 3.5 Flash shows that teams happy with 3.0 Flash aren't willing to pay the higher cost yet.

Conclusion: Cost-effective, capable options mean smarter model mixes

This month's report signals increased pricing sensitivity in the market, even as overall spend and token volume grow. That means developers are looking for ways to get more out of every dollar.

Data revealed two optimization strategies:

  1. Using DeepSeek's cheap, but capable V4 family for lower-risk, high-volume tasks

  2. Choosing to delay model family upgrades until the ROI makes sense

Routing gives teams the ability to adjust their model mix, and budget, in real time as the labs compete for different layers of production AI workloads.

Appendix

Token vs cost share by B2B classification

B2B applications run fewer, more expensive calls, while B2C applications run many cheap ones. On a per-token basis, B2B cost roughly 60% more than B2C in May.

Agent tool use across tokens and requests

Just under a quarter of requests end in a tool call, but those requests carry well over half of all tokens. Both metrics are roughly flat month-over-month.

Model diversity distribution by request volume

The more requests an app serves, the more models it runs in production. Single-model setups dominate the lowest-volume tier, while at 1M+ requests the majority of apps route across 11 or more models.

Cost vs volume share by use case

Use case cost share indicates how expensive a wrong answer is, not how many tokens it burns. Personal assistants and coding agents run cheap per token, while back-office and recruiting work costs far more.

Previous reports

Read the May 2026 AI Gateway production index.

About this data

This analysis is based on anonymized, aggregate routing data from the Vercel AI Gateway through May 2026.

A few notes on measurement:

  • Spend uses market-rate pricing (published list price) to provide a normalized view across teams that bring their own API keys.

  • Volume counts tokens routed through AI Gateway.

  • B2C, B2B, and use-case classifications are aggregate. No individual team or workload is identified.

  • All figures use the most recent data available; prior months may be revised as data completes.

Using AI Gateway to integrate multiple providers with one API key

Running agent workflows in Vercel Sandboxes

The findings are passed to a coding agent, which opens a pull request with the fix, ready for the developer to review and merge. Detection, analysis, code change: the entire loop runs automatically, with a human making the final call before anything goes live.

Okara adopted Vercel Sandboxes the day they launched. Rizwan saw the announcement on X and the team started building immediately.

What's next

120,000 websites are now using Okara's AI CMO. The team ships to production six or seven times a day, and every improvement lands for customers the same day it ships. Okara is expanding its agent suite and moving upmarket to serve larger teams. As the product grows, so does the infrastructure demand. More users, more agents, more tokens. When you're four people handling growth for 120,000 companies, you can't afford for infrastructure to be a distraction. With Vercel, it isn't.

title: Start Here: What Happens When AI Makes Your Thinking Visible
description:
Every tool humans have built records the product of thinking.

A document records what you concluded. A commit records what you shipped. A photograph records what you saw. All of them keep the destination and throw away the route.

AI is the first medium that keeps the route.

A conversation with a model preserves what you were trying to do, which approaches you ruled out and why, which objection actually changed your mind, and where you started drifting. For the first time, the path of a thought has an external record.

That single change is what this series is about. I call that record process information.

The AI Thought Quartet is eight articles in two parts. Part I asks what this change does to thinking. Part II asks what you do about it.

Below is the whole argument, and where each article sits in it.

At a glance:

# Part Article Answers In one line
1 I AI Is Not a Smarter Search Engine What is it? The path of a thought gets an external record
2 I Code Can Be Committed — But Who Owns the Thinking? Who owns it? Tool defaults are political
3 I From Recording Conversations to "Resurrecting" Thought What is it good for? The hard part was never collection — it's interpretation
4 I The Reflector of Thought, the Accelerator of Civilization What does it mean? Countless mirrors, gathered, become a furnace
5 II · Sovereignty You Fear Your Boss Reading Your AI Chats. Nvidia Fears Anthropic Reading Its Chips. The landscape The fear at every layer has the same shape
6 II · Sovereignty Old Security Guards the Vault. New Security Guards the Stream. The battlefield What's protected changed from a stored asset to a flowing process
7 II · Practice AI Is Not a Faster Keyboard The method What changes is never the method — it's the instrument
8 II · Practice The World Is Not an Arena The mindset Every sovereignty rests on one person's command over their own thinking

Part I asks what AI changes. In Part II, Sovereignty is about who holds the record and Practice is about what you do with it.

Part I — What AI changes

Four questions, in order.

1. What is it?

AI Is Not a Smarter Search Engine — It's a Mirror for Your Thinking

A search engine matches information that already exists. It creates nothing and leaves no trace — you walk away with an answer, and your thinking is exactly where it was. A conversation with a model is the opposite: it clarifies, challenges, and reorganizes, and the whole exchange stays behind.

This is where the series starts, and where "process information" gets its footing. It is also the lowest-friction read of the eight.

2. Who owns it?

Code Can Be Committed — But Who Owns the Thinking?

Code can be committed, attributed, and reviewed. The conversation that produced it cannot. Leave the defaults alone, and every thinking process your team generates quietly becomes company property — not through malice, but because nobody ever decided otherwise.

The argument here is not that companies are villains. It is that tool defaults are political. Whatever a tool does by default is the power structure you will end up living in.

3. What is it good for?

From Recording Conversations to "Resurrecting" Thought

What humanity actually kept from its own past is much thinner than we assume. The earliest records we have are not philosophy — they are grain tallies and debt. This article traces the archiving tradition forward and asks what AI adds to it.

The honest answer is that the hard part was never collection. It is interpretation.

4. What does it mean?

The Reflector of Thought, the Accelerator of Civilization

Zoom all the way out. Countless private thought archives, reflected and gathered together, stop being mirrors and become a furnace.

Part I ends on a question it deliberately does not answer: if fragments of thought are going to converge, under what terms? Part II is the answer.

Part II — What you do about it

Part II splits into two halves, and it reads differently from Part I on purpose. Each of its four articles comes out of a different discipline: compute and supply chains, data security, the scientific method, and education. Part I is diagnosis. Part II is practice.

The Sovereignty half — who holds the record

You Fear Your Boss Reading Your AI Chats. Nvidia Fears Anthropic Reading Its Chips.

It opens with a story that is genuinely strange. Nvidia — the company pushing AI hardest, earning the most from it, and holding equity in the model vendor on the other side — pulled its own employees off a frontier model. If the player with the most to gain and the least reason to admit a problem still felt it necessary to defend itself, the rest of us should look at the structure.

That structure turns out to have four layers, and the same fear at every one: I supplied the core resource, and the process information was intercepted one level up.

Old Security Guards the Vault. New Security Guards the Stream.

Written from inside the data-security industry. The model most of us learned — data at rest, in transit, in use — was built for things you can store and lock. Process information is not stored; it leaks while in use, and it reconstructs more truth than any customer table.

The two layers this article adds on top of the standard three are the author's own proposal, and it says so plainly rather than passing them off as industry consensus.

The Practice half — what to do with it

AI Is Not a Faster Keyboard — It's a Microscope for Your Own Mind

If Part I's image was a mirror, this is the same instrument turned around. The scientific method's loop — observe, hypothesize, verify, correct — has not changed in centuries. What changes is the instrument of observation, and we now have one pointed at our own thinking.

Two lines in this article are the author's own practice, stated plainly: he kept the conversations and went back to them, and he records his meetings and has AI walk through them afterward.

The World Is Not an Arena — It's an Open-World RPG

The series closes at its smallest scale, not its largest. After seven articles about sovereignty, security, and civilization, the last one asks how you see the world — and what you would pass on to a child.

There is a reason it ends here: every layer of sovereignty above an individual rests on that individual's command over their own thinking process.

How the two parts connect

Four joints hold the eight articles together.

Article 2 → Article 5. Article 2 raises the question of who owns one person's thinking process. Article 5 starts with the author's own year-old worry about exactly that, then scales it up through four layers. He is explicit that his original worry was not misplaced — only too low in the stack.

Article 3 → Article 6. Article 3 is about the archive. Article 6 says the archive changed shape: from a stored asset (the vault) to a flowing process (the stream). The security model built for the old shape does not cover the new one.

Article 1 → Article 7. The mirror in article 1 and the microscope in article 7 are the same instrument — one pointed at what the AI is doing, the other at how you yourself think.

Article 4 → Article 8. Article 4 pulls the camera out to civilization. Article 8 pulls it back to a single person. The series deliberately does not end at the grand scale.

Where to start

Each article stands alone, but they are written to be read in order.

  • If you read one: article 1, then article 5. That pair carries the core of the argument.
  • If you work in security: article 6, then article 2.
  • If you are here for your own practice: articles 7 and 8.
  • If you want the full argument: 1 → 8, in order.

The anchor

The series is not purely theoretical. It grew out of a real tool — ai-tracedoc, an MIT-licensed Claude Code plugin that records your development process into a local Markdown ledger. Local by default, voluntary, no admin back office.

No More Documentation Debt: A Claude Code Plugin That Records Your Dev Process

The plugin is the reason the argument has somewhere to land. Every claim in these eight articles is one I had to test against something I was actually building.

If the series is useful to you, the tool is the part you can run.

Part I was published September 2026 as **The AI Thought Quartet. Part II followed as **The AI Thought Quartet, Part II: Sovereignty and Practice.

title: AI Stock Trading: Equities Reality, Session Costs, and What the Model Should Never Decide
description:
AI Stock Trading: Equities Reality, Session Costs, and What the Model Should Never Decide

AI stock trading means three unrelated products sharing one label: a screener that ranks tickers and leaves the decision to you; a chat assistant that answers questions about your account when asked; and software that forms a view, commits capital without asking, then finds out whether it was right. Only the third changes how a position gets taken. The distinction is not sophistication. It is whether the system ever learns what happened after its own decision.

This article is educational, not investment advice. Trading involves risk of loss. Nothing here is a performance claim.

Table of contents

  • What AI stock trading actually means
  • How it differs from bots, desks, and chat assistants
  • Buying checklist for equities and ETF AI claims
  • Session reality: gaps, costs, calendars, and failure modes
  • Comparison: screener vs chat tool vs AI trading system
  • Common mistakes and red flags
  • Who should and should not use AI stock trading software
  • FAQ
  • Where TradeAgentic fits

What AI stock trading actually means

In equities, “AI” is useful in a narrow set of jobs and dangerous when asked to do arithmetic or loss bounding. Language models excel at reading filings, disclosures, transcripts, and announcements that arrive in no fixed shape. They can hold several considerations at once—a disclosure against a calendar against an existing position—and produce an argument rather than a score. Constructing the strongest case not to act is often more valuable than constructing the case for acting, because most candidates should not be taken.

What AI should not own:

  • Exact arithmetic — position sizing, what a stop implies, what a spread costs. Language models are unreliable at exact calculation and inconsistent across identical inputs. That work belongs in deterministic code, checked before an order exists.
  • Loss bounds — a control that depends on a model producing the same output twice is not a control. Daily loss limits, protective orders, and the rule that halts the day have to be code that cannot be talked out of firing.
  • Its own confidence — a model asked for a view will produce one whether or not the evidence supports it. Confidence has to be established by grading past decisions against outcomes, not by asking the model how sure it is.

Inputs worth having are more than price: the market’s own record of what traded; company filings and insider disclosures; earnings dates, dividends, index changes, and economic releases; news and other text, used carefully so the system only acts on what was knowable at decision time. Research that quietly uses information from after the decision will look brilliant and mean nothing. For how language-model agents fit a desk loop, see LLM trading agents.

How it differs from bots, desks, and chat assistants

Screener or ranking tool. Scores a list. You decide. The model never sees the outcome of your trade unless someone builds that loop.

Chat assistant. Answers when asked. May even place an order on request. It is a tool with a conversational interface, not autonomy.

AI stock trading bot. Often a rule bot with an AI label, or a prediction bot that trades a forecast. See the dedicated bot taxonomy on AI stock trading bot.

Automated / agentic desk. Forms a view, argues against candidates, acts inside hard limits, reconciles to the broker, and grades decisions—including refusals—against subsequent market outcomes.

The SERP job for AI stock trading is equities-specific: session hours, overnight gaps, borrow and short rules where relevant, PDT and margin regimes as your broker applies them, and the cost of being wrong in names with wide spreads. A crypto-first pitch or a futures HFT pitch is answering a different question.

Buying checklist for equities and ETF AI claims

  1. What exactly does the AI decide? Which stocks, when, how much—or nothing at all?
  2. Where does it run, and who holds the keys? Your machine with OS keychain storage, or a vendor database.
  3. Does it record declines with reasons? Fills alone are half the evidence.
  4. Can you rerun research with realistic costs? Spreads, commissions, and slippage—not mid-price fantasy.
  5. How is look-ahead prevented? Models may “know” what happened after a backtest date because that period was in training data. Equities research with LLMs must be built so the model cannot draw on knowledge from after the point being tested.
  6. What happens to open positions if software or vendor disappears? Broker-resident protection is the only acceptable answer for overnight equity risk.
  7. Which limits can the system never change? Written down, not implied. See agentic trading risk controls.
  8. Is paper mode unlimited? You need dull weeks, volatile weeks, and a restart.
  9. Does it know the earnings and event calendar? Many of the worst equity surprises arrive on dates that were known in advance.
  10. How does it treat thinly traded names? Wide spreads and sudden gaps make every order expensive and every stop less reliable.
  11. Does sizing live in deterministic code? If the model picks share count by prose, walk away.
  12. Who is the regulated party? Orders should go through your registered broker-dealer. Software that tries to route around your broker should worry you.

Session reality: gaps, costs, calendars, and failure modes

US equities and ETFs trade in a defined weekday session. That sounds basic until automation meets the calendar.

Overnight and weekend gaps. A position held after the close can open far from the prior print. Protective orders resting at the broker still matter; they do not guarantee a fill at the stop price in a gap. Software that implies otherwise is marketing.

Halts and limit-up / limit-down. Trading can stop without warning. Orders may not fill; protection may fill far from its price. A well-built system stands aside when its data or the market stops making sense.

Stale quotes and wide markets. Near the open, around news, and in less liquid names, the book can be thin. Acting on numbers the system cannot verify is guessing with confidence. Refuse and say so on screen.

Cost model honesty. Frictionless fills and mid-price assumptions turn mediocre equity systems into impressive charts. Commissions, spreads, and market impact on size produce less flattering and far more useful numbers.

Scheduled events. Earnings, dividends, index reconstitutions, and macro releases are cheap protection when known and expensive surprises when ignored. AI that “reads the news” but does not respect the calendar is incomplete for stocks.

Day-trading and margin regimes. Pattern day trader rules for margin accounts were replaced in 2026 in the US, and brokers may phase changes differently. Confirm which regime your account is on before relying on anything written about day-trading limits. The software does not change who is responsible for the account.

Failure mode: confident wrong arithmetic. An LLM proposes a size that violates a concentration cap or leaves no room for a protective order. Correct architecture: the model may argue; code sizes and refuses.

Failure mode: look-ahead in research. A narrative summary of a filing that was not yet public on the simulated decision date. Correct architecture: time-aware inputs only.

Failure mode: vendor outage with equity overnight risk. Hosted decisioning goes dark while the position remains. Correct architecture: broker-resident stops and a kill switch you can operate independently of the vendor’s UI.

Comparison: screener vs chat tool vs AI trading system

Dimension Screener / ranker Chat assistant AI stock trading system
Who decides You You (when you ask) The software
Sees the outcome No No Yes, and scores it
Records refusals No No Yes, with reasons
Changes over time Only when retrained Prompt / vendor update From its own graded record
Where it typically runs Vendor servers Vendor servers Your machine, ideally
Equity calendar awareness Sometimes If you ask Should be built in
Owns sizing No Risky if yes Deterministic code only
Overnight protection story N/A N/A Broker-resident required

Common mistakes and red flags

Buying a chatbot and calling it trading. Answering questions is not committing capital and grading the result.

Letting the model size or set stops in prose. Arithmetic and loss bounds belong in code.

Win rates without costs. Especially toxic in equities where spreads and gaps dominate small edges.

Ignoring liquidity. Heavily traded names have tight spreads; thinly traded names punish automation even when the view is right.

Drifting from paper to live. Moving to real money should be a decision on a specific day for specific reasons, not a setting you slide into.

Unread decision records. The balance tells you how the market went. The decision record tells you whether the system did what it said. Only one is evidence about the software.

AI presented as the reason it will win. Autonomy and intelligence describe how something decides, not whether it is right.

Who should and should not use AI stock trading software

Suitable when: you trade US equities/ETFs (and possibly options or crypto under the same envelope) and want continuous judgment inside hard limits; you will run paper long enough to see session quirks; you accept that AI helps with unstructured reading and argument, not with magic prediction; you will set daily loss, concentration, and kill-switch controls before live size.

Not suitable when: you need approval on every order; you want guaranteed returns or “AI predicts the market”; you will not read refusals and reconciliations; you expect a chat box to replace risk code; your market is outside what the product actually supports.

Start from the homepage overview at tradeagentic.ai if you are still mapping product shape, then return to equities-specific evaluation here.

FAQ

What is AI stock trading?

Three different products share the label: a screener that ranks tickers, a chat assistant that answers questions about your account, and software that forms a view, commits capital without asking, and then grades the result. Only the third is autonomous. The test is whether the system ever finds out what happened after its own decision.

Does AI stock trading actually work?

Some of it does something useful and most of it is a scoring model behind a subscription. The question that separates them is whether the system learns what happened after its decision and changes as a result. No honest vendor will tell you it wins, and any that does is selling the wrong thing.

Should AI decide how much to buy?

No. Sizing is arithmetic. Language models are unreliable at exact calculation and inconsistent across identical inputs. Anything determining how much capital moves, what a protective stop implies, or what a spread costs belongs in deterministic code checked before an order exists.

Where should AI stock trading software run?

On your own machine with your own broker credentials, if you can choose. Software deciding on a vendor’s servers makes their outage, their breach, and their retraining schedule into risks to your account, and turns your trading activity into their telemetry.

Can AI predict the stock market?

Not reliably, and nothing credible claims to. What AI does well in equities is read large amounts of unstructured information, weigh several considerations at once, and argue the case against a trade. Prediction is not the product. Discipline, recording, and grading are.

Is AI stock trading legal?

Yes. Using software to trade your own brokerage account is legal, and the same rules apply as when you trade by hand. Orders pass through a registered broker, which applies margin and other requirements. A software licensor is not your adviser and does not hold your money.

Is AI stock trading safe?

No trading is safe, and AI does not make losses impossible. What makes it safer is limits that sit outside the AI: protective orders resting at the broker, a hard daily loss limit, a control that closes everything at once, and a refusal to trade when its own checks fail.

How do I start with AI stock trading?

On a paper account, with limits set before the first trade. Run it long enough to see ordinary days, volatile days, and a restart; read what it decided and declined; move to real money deliberately and at a smaller size than feels necessary.

Where TradeAgentic fits

TradeAgentic is a native macOS and Windows AI agentic trading desk for operators who run it themselves. For equities and ETFs—and also options and crypto—it forms views, argues against candidates, runs pre-trade risk checks, records and grades refusals, and keeps protective stops at the broker. Kill switch, daily loss stop, and concentration caps sit outside discretionary override. Credentials stay in the OS keychain via your brokerage API. Consumer and enterprise licensing are available. Educational use; not investment advice.

For the equities-focused product outline, see AI stock trading. For model role boundaries, see LLM trading agents. For hard controls, see agentic trading risk controls.

This content is for education only. It is not investment advice. Past or hypothetical results are not guarantees. You can lose money trading. TradeAgentic does not manage your money and does not provide personalized investment advice.

title: Automated Trading Desk: The Full Job Set a Bot and Platform Do Not Cover
description:
Automated Trading Desk: The Full Job Set a Bot and Platform Do Not Cover

An automated trading desk is software that performs the continuous work of a trading desk without a person approving each decision: watching the market, forming a view, arguing against candidates, sizing, routing, confirming protection at the broker, reconciling to the brokerage record, and grading what it did—including refusals. Most products sold into this category do two or three of those jobs and leave the rest to you. That gap is where evenings go, and it is the difference between buying order placement and buying a desk.

This article is educational, not investment advice. Trading involves risk of loss. Nothing here is a performance claim.

Table of contents

  • What an automated trading desk is
  • How a desk differs from a bot, a platform, and a staffed desk
  • Buying checklist: twelve questions that survive a sales call
  • Architecture and workflow: where desks fail
  • Comparison: bot vs platform vs automated desk
  • Common mistakes and red flags
  • Who should and should not use an automated trading desk
  • FAQ
  • Where TradeAgentic fits

What an automated trading desk is

An automated trading desk is software that covers the full set of desk jobs on a continuous schedule, not a single strategy and not an order router. The word desk is doing real work in that sentence. On a traditional desk, separate people form the view, check risk, place orders, reconcile books, and keep the operation inside the rules. An automated desk performs those same functions in software on one machine. The jobs do not go away. What changes is who performs them, how often, and what gets written down.

Four functions decide whether the label is honest:

  1. View formation — deciding what is worth taking and, far more often, what is not.
  2. Independent risk check — sizing and exposure checked before capital moves, with authority to stop the order.
  3. Operations — confirming fills, matching positions and fees to the broker, and resolving disagreements.
  4. Governance — staying inside account restrictions, margin rules, and the limits the owner set.

A product that only places orders when a signal fires is automation. A product that covers all four and records refusals as carefully as fills is closer to a desk. For the narrower definition of continuous judgment with grading, see what is agentic trading.

How a desk differs from a bot, a platform, and a staffed desk

These terms are sold as synonyms. They are not.

A trading bot executes a judgment somebody made once. You define conditions; the software watches for them and acts when they occur. Faithful repetition is exactly what you want from execution. The weakness is that nothing revisits the instruction when the regime changes, and the software has no way of noticing.

A trading platform gives you tools and a screen. It is genuinely useful and it is a different purchase. Judgment still happens when you are sitting in front of it.

A staffed desk is a room of people with separate jobs. Coverage thins when someone is away. Refusals are rarely kept. Accountability sits with named individuals.

An automated trading desk keeps operating when you are not there. It forms the view itself, argues against candidates before capital moves, and scores what it decided against what the market then did—including the refusals. Refusing is the majority of the work on a disciplined desk. If a product only shows fills, you are looking at automation with a new label.

The last row in any honest comparison matters most: automating the desk does not automate responsibility. Someone still owns the account, sets the limits, reads the record, and decides whether to keep running it. The software removes the approval step, not the owner.

Buying checklist: twelve questions that survive a sales call

Ask these in order. Treat a missing or vague answer as an answer.

  1. Where does the decision run? On your machine with your keys, or on a vendor’s servers. If theirs, their outage, their breach, and their solvency become risks to your account.
  2. Where does protection rest? A stop held inside the software disappears when the software does. One resting at the brokerage survives a crash, a reboot, a power cut, and the vendor disappearing. See agentic trading risk controls for the control set that should sit beyond the reach of automation.
  3. Can you read the refusals? Any product will show fills. The candidates it declined, and why, are where you find out whether judgment is real rather than asserted.
  4. Does it reconcile to the broker before new risk opens? Positions close overnight, somebody intervenes, a process restarts. A desk that reports from its own database is reporting intentions. Realized profit and fees have to be rebuilt from the broker’s own record.
  5. What stops the day, and can the software widen it? An autonomous system needs a fixed loss threshold, checked before every order, and not adjustable by any automated part of the system.
  6. Is there a kill switch that flattens everything immediately? One control that cancels open orders and closes positions belongs in the non-negotiable set.
  7. Are concentration caps hard? Limits on how large any one name or cluster may become should not be soft suggestions the decision layer can talk past.
  8. Can you reproduce the research? A backtest you cannot rerun on your own hardware, with a real cost model rather than frictionless fills, is a sales asset rather than evidence.
  9. What happens on restart with a position open? Clean resumption—reconcile positions and protection first, then decide—is an unattended requirement, not a nice-to-have.
  10. What does it do on stale or implausible data? Standing aside and saying so on screen is correct behavior. Trading through a feed glitch is not.
  11. Is there unlimited paper mode? You need ordinary weeks, volatile weeks, and at least one restart before real money.
  12. What do you keep if you stop paying or the vendor stops? Licensed software you operate is a different resilience model than a subscription that goes dark with the company.

Architecture and workflow: where desks fail

A serious desk is not a strategy with a broker plug-in. It is a pipeline with gates. Concrete failure modes show up in the same places across products.

Startup gate failure. The process comes up, sees an open position in its own database, and opens new risk before confirming what the broker actually holds and whether protection is still resting. Correct behavior: reconcile positions and protective orders first; refuse new risk until the books match.

Protection that lived in memory. The machine reboots or the process dies. Software-held stops vanish. Broker-resident stops remain. If the product cannot demonstrate broker-resident protection for the instruments it trades, treat overnight and weekend exposure as uninsured.

Partial fills and orphan legs. Multi-leg options and busy sessions produce partials. A desk that assumes every intended fill arrived will size the next order wrong and may leave an unbalanced book. Operations must treat the broker’s fill record as source of truth.

Credential and session expiry. API tokens expire. The desk must fail closed—no new orders—rather than retry into a broken session while pretending it is still protected.

Regime drift without a grader. View formation that never scores refusals and fills against subsequent market outcomes cannot tell a working approach from a lucky stretch. Grading is not a dashboard vanity; it is the only honest input for later allocation across strategies competing for one capital pool. Related design patterns appear in multi-agent trading systems.

Operator machine hygiene. Sleep, automatic OS updates, and a shared family laptop are operational risks. A dedicated machine that stays on, with sleep and disruptive updates controlled, is part of the architecture, not an afterthought. Overnight positions still carry risk; the only protection that counts is the kind resting at the brokerage.

A normal day from the operator’s side. Before the session: look for a readiness message, not an approval queue. During the session: you can watch or not; decisions appear including declines. After the close: spend a few minutes matching figures to the broker and reading refusals. Once a week: review what the desk changed about itself and the evidence behind each change.

Comparison: bot vs platform vs automated desk

Dimension Trading bot Trading platform Automated trading desk
Who formed the view A person, once A person, each time The software, continuously
Refusals Absence of a signal Not recorded Recorded and graded
When conditions change Keeps firing You intervene Reprices the view
Protection Often in software Varies Resting at the broker
Reconciliation Rarely Sometimes Before any new order
Hours covered Rule schedule While you are present Every session the machine runs
Record of judgment Rules file Your memory Decision log with outcomes
Accountability You plus the rule You Operator who runs it

Staffed versus automated is a second table worth keeping separate: staffed desks scale with people; automated desks scale with markets on the same machine. Neither removes the need for a named owner of the account and the limits.

Common mistakes and red flags

Confusing coverage with sophistication. Hours of uptime and a long feature list do not mean the software covers risk, reconciliation, and grading. Judge it on the four desk functions.

Expecting an approval queue. There is no approval step in a genuine desk. If being consulted on every order matters, a signal service or screener will serve better and cost less.

Treating autonomy as a performance claim. Autonomy is a statement about who decides, not about accuracy. Any vendor presenting autonomy as an edge is selling the wrong thing.

Skipping paper and tiny size. Run until you have watched refusals, recovery from a restart with a position open, and behavior through a day you did not expect. Early live size should be a fraction of full intent.

Using a shared or sleeping machine. Dedicated always-on hardware is an operating requirement for unattended equities and especially for crypto sessions that never close.

Accepting win-rate marketing. Screenshots of profitable days, returns without costs, and “AI” as the reason it will win are red flags. Ask for the written statement of what the system will never do.

Password instead of limited API key. A request for full brokerage login credentials rather than scoped API access is a reason to walk away.

Who should and should not use an automated trading desk

Suitable when: you want positions taken while you are not watching; you care more about process discipline and an audit trail than approving individual trades; you will keep a machine running and read the record on a cadence; you are willing to set hard loss, concentration, and kill-switch limits before the first live order; firms that must answer to an allocator or trustee for why the system did something.

Not suitable when: you need to approve each trade; you expect “AI” or autonomy to mean higher accuracy; nobody will operate the machine or read the record; you want a hosted subscription with zero operational burden (a hosted platform may be the honest answer); you are shopping for a screener or chat assistant and calling it a desk.

Enterprise buyers evaluating multi-user governance, capital pools, and licensing should also review enterprise AI trading software.

FAQ

What is an automated trading desk?

Software that performs the jobs of a trading desk without a person approving each decision: watching the market, forming and arguing against views, sizing and routing orders, confirming protection rests at the broker, reconciling to the brokerage record, and grading its own decisions afterwards—including refusals. Most products marketed this way do a few of those jobs and leave the rest to you.

How is an automated trading desk different from a trading bot?

A bot executes a judgment a person made once and has no way of noticing when that judgment stops working. A desk forms the view itself, argues against it before committing, and scores what it decided against what the market then did. The difference is not sophistication; it is whether anything revisits the instruction.

Can one person run an automated trading desk?

Yes, provided the software genuinely covers the unattended jobs rather than only order placement. The parts that decide it are automatic reconciliation to the broker, verified protection before new risk is opened, and clean resumption after a restart—those are what otherwise land on a person at inconvenient hours.

What should an automated trading desk show me before I buy?

A record of what it refused as well as what it traded; how figures on screen are reconciled against the broker’s own record; the written statement of what the system will never do; and research you can reproduce on your own machine with realistic costs.

Does an automated trading desk run overnight and on weekends?

It runs whenever the machine is on and the market it trades is open. US equities trade on weekdays during set hours; crypto trades around the clock. Positions held overnight should be protected by orders resting at the brokerage so protection holds even if the computer does not.

Is an automated trading desk the same as high-frequency trading?

No. High-frequency trading competes on speed and needs infrastructure next to the exchange. An automated trading desk is about who makes the decisions and whether they are recorded and graded. Speed is not the proposition.

What does it cost to run an automated trading desk?

Three things: the software license, a dedicated computer that stays on, and your own brokerage account. The useful comparison is against the functions a staffed desk needs, not against one trader’s time alone.

Who is accountable when the desk is automated?

The operator who owns the account, sets the limits, and decides whether to keep running it. Automation removes the per-trade approval step, not responsibility.

Where TradeAgentic fits

TradeAgentic is a native macOS and Windows AI agentic trading desk—not a browser dashboard. Multiple strategies compete for one capital pool. Candidates are argued against before funding. Pre-trade risk checks run before capital moves. Refusals are recorded and graded against what the market did. Protective stops sit at the broker; a kill switch, daily loss stop, and concentration caps sit outside discretionary override. It connects to your own brokerage API for equities and ETFs, options, and crypto. Credentials stay in the OS keychain. Consumer and enterprise licensing are available.

If you want software that covers the desk’s jobs rather than only order placement, start with the automated trading desk overview, and for firm-level controls review enterprise AI trading software and agentic trading risk controls. Decide whether the record it keeps is one you are willing to read.
